Abstract
Autonomous ecological monitoring requires robotic systems capable of efficiently exploring large natural environments while minimizing redundant traversal under limited communication and partial environmental knowledge. Although reinforcement learning provides adaptive decision making for multi-robot exploration, sparse rewards often result in inefficient exploration and slow policy convergence. This paper investigates whether locality-preserving geometric priors can improve decentralized reinforcement learning for ecological monitoring. We incorporate Hilbert space-filling curve information through state augmentation, exploration biasing, and potential-based reward shaping while preserving the underlying reinforcement learning algorithms. The framework is implemented using Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and evaluated in simulated multi-robot ecological survey environments using teams of 4–16 robots. Performance is evaluated using coverage ratio, redundancy, cumulative reward, convergence speed, and ablation studies. The experimental evaluation presented in this section demonstrates consistent improvements in reinforcement learning-based coverage performance through the incorporation of Hilbert-guided structured exploration. Across all evaluated simulation environments and robot team sizes, both H-DQN and H-PPO achieved higher coverage ratios and lower redundancy than their corresponding baseline reinforcement learning algorithms.

4. Discussion
4.1. Interpretation of the experimental findings
The primary objective of this study was to investigate whether incorporating locality-preserving geometric priors into reinforcement learning improves exploration efficiency for decentralized multi-robot coverage. The experimental results presented in
Section 3
consistently support this hypothesis. Across all evaluated environments, Hilbert-guided structured exploration produced higher coverage ratios, lower redundancy, faster convergence, and greater cumulative reward than the corresponding baseline reinforcement learning algorithms. These improvements were observed for both value-based (H-DQN) and policy-gradient (H-PPO) methods, indicating that the proposed framework is largely independent of the underlying reinforcement

proach to future autonomous robotic systems designed for long-duration ecological monitoring and ecosystem restoration.
4.4. Limitations
Although the proposed framework demonstrated consistent improvements in coverage efficiency and learning performance across the evaluated experiments, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results.
First, the proposed framework does not implement explicit inter-robot communication or centralized coordination. Each robot makes decisions independently using locally available observations together with the Hilbert-guided exploration mechanism. Consequently, the reduction in coverage redundancy observed throughout the experiments should not be interpreted as evidence of explicit cooperative planning. Instead, the results indicate that locality-preserving geometric priors can improve decentralized exploration efficiency even in the absence of communi

ation offers an efficient mechanism for systematically acquiring spatial information over extended operational periods.
5. Conclusion
This study investigated the use of locality-preserving geometric priors to improve reinforcement learning for decentralized multi-robot ecological monitoring. The motivation for this work was the observation that reinforcement learning often suffers from inefficient exploration and slow policy convergence in large-scale coverage tasks, while classical coverage path planning algorithms generally lack the adaptability required for dynamic or partially known natural environments. To address these challenges, we introduced a lightweight framework that incorporates Hilbert space-filling curve priors through state augmentation, exploration biasing, and potential-based reward shaping while preserving the underlying reinforcement learning algorithms.
